summary:
Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.

Same-sex marriage reached Réunion with the metropolitan statute adopted in 2013, following the bill announced by Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault in October 2012 for passage through the National Assembly and the Senate.

Discrimination on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' has been prosecutable in France since the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 in July 2012, which made transphobic harassment a criminal matter. The provision is in force in Réunion.

Legal gender change rests on the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted by the National Assembly on 19 May 2016 after being tabled by roughly forty Socialist deputies. Three government sub-amendments tabled alongside it could narrow its scope, and the sources do not establish the final wording.

Detention is the sharpest documented exposure. Under article D248 of the criminal procedure code, prisoners are placed according to the sex recorded on their identity documents, which leaves transgender women held in male prisons in a legal grey area. BuzzFeed News reported on 12 January 2018 that such women are punished for considerably more than their alleged crimes, following cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid threats from other inmates.

The French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL) issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding the persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities. Its findings rest on referrals received since 2010 covering some forty transgender people, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site and documentary inspections, and it issued recommendations to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. The opinion addresses the national custody framework that covers Réunion.

No local violence series, enforcement pattern or institutional hostility programme appears in the sources, and equally no documented local support infrastructure; a small, discreet community should be assumed but is not evidenced.
tangentialFactors:
The 2012 marriage and adoption bill drew open opposition from the Catholic Bishops Conference to the adoption provision, evidence of organised institutional resistance at the moment the reform entered the legislative process.

The protections in force in Réunion are metropolitan statutes extended by departmental status rather than locally enacted measures, so enforcement evidence from mainland facilities is the nearest available proxy for what a trans visitor or resident would encounter in custody on the island.

The detention findings are national in scope and issued by an independent supervisory body, not a local authority: the CGLPL opinion and the BuzzFeed reporting describe a systemic placement problem rather than a Réunion-specific programme.

Legislative scope was contested at the point of adoption in both 2012 and 2016, in the first case over adoption and in the second over government sub-amendments capable of limiting legal gender change.
localsOnly:
Residents may petition for legal gender change under the Civil Code section created by amendment 282 in 2016, though the limits the government's three sub-amendments placed on that section are not resolved in the sources.

Discrimination complaints founded on 'identité sexuelle' proceed under Penal Code article L225-1 as amended in July 2012, giving residents a criminal-law route against transphobic harassment.

Residents held in custody are placed by the sex on their identity documents under article D248 of the criminal procedure code, and the CGLPL recommendations of 25 May 2021 are addressed to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries, which administer that framework nationwide.

The 2012 parliamentary record shows deputies Sergio Coronado (EELV) and Elisabeth Pochon (PS) intervening in the debate that added 'identité sexuelle' to the penal code, and the bill was put to the National Assembly and Senate as a commitment of President Hollande's campaign.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the CGLPL referrals received since 2010 concerned a facility in Réunion is not sourced; the opinion covers French custody facilities as a whole and does not break its roughly forty cases down by territory.

The final text and practical scope of the 2016 legal gender change section, after the government's three sub-amendments, remain unresolved in the sources.

No sourced data exists on local support organisations, incidents of violence against trans people, or enforcement outcomes under article L225-1 in Réunion specifically.

Whether a corrected identity document changes actual prison placement under article D248 in practice is unresolved; the reporting describes a legal grey area rather than a settled rule.

The procedure and availability of gender-marker changes on identity documents issued in Réunion are not covered by the inventory.
